title: Make it yours
one: Turning the bike shop into your own case study: copy each part, then change the names.
marks: This chapter is where the bike shop becomes your own project. The examiner gives the marks for your own case study, built with the same rules as the bike shop: no double booking, stock that is always right, and a refusal in a plain sentence.

stages.title: Match your own tables to the bike shop

screens.title: See what you will do in this chapter.

blocks.p: You have built the whole bike shop: the script, the stored procedures and the program. Your own case study uses the same shapes with different names on them, so you do not start from nothing.

This chapter shows one method that turns each part of the bike shop into a part of your own project: copy the bike shop part, then change the names. The checks, the IF lines and the order of the lines stay the same, because the rules are the same.

box.title: What stays and what changes
box.text: The rules stay: the clash check, the IF NOT EXISTS check before every change, @Message with its refusal sentence, and RETURN. The names change: the tables, the columns, the @ names, the stored procedure names and the words in each sentence.

blocks.p: Chapters 1 to 9 each have a Make it yours box that says what to build in your own project. Work through those boxes in order, one chapter at a time, using the method in this chapter.

screens.title: Sort out your own tables first.

blocks.p: Read your case study and write down the nouns in it, the way chapter 2 did for the bike shop. Then put each of your tables beside the bike shop table with the same shape. Do this before you copy anything.

box.title: The ten bike shop tables, by shape
box.text: Booked by time: Appointment. Booked by day: Hire. Counted stock: Part, with PartOrder and PartSale. One-off stock: Bike. The people and the lists: Customer, Staff, Supplier and ServiceType.

blocks.p: A driving school, for example, books lessons by the hour, so its Lesson table copies Appointment and its Instructor table copies Staff. A case study may not use all four shapes. Copy only the shapes yours has.
Each table you copy brings its own stored procedures, its own class in Models, its own data class and its own screens. Stage 2 shows how to copy them.

screens.title: Copy one stored procedure and change its names.

blocks.p: Find the stored procedure in BikeShop.sql that does the same job as the action you want in your own case study. Its name is the table and then the action, such as usp_Appointment_Cancel. Copy it into your own script, the one chapter 1 told you to name for your case study. Then change its names, as the parts below show.
Below is usp_Appointment_Cancel from the bike shop, part by part. Each part says what a driving school would change and what it would keep.

code.title: usp_Appointment_Cancel: what changes and what stays
parts: CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_Appointment_Cancel
@Message VARCHAR(200) OUTPUT
The name and what goes in: change these

usp_Appointment_Cancel becomes usp_Lesson_Cancel, and @AppointmentID becomes @LessonID. @Message stays exactly as it is, because every stored procedure that changes data sends its sentence back in @Message.

SET @Message = '';
AS, BEGIN and the blank message: keep these
These three lines are the same in every stored procedure that changes data. Nothing in them belongs to the bike shop.

The check: keep the shape, change the names

The check stays: if there is no open booking with this number, the sentence goes back and RETURN stops. Appointment becomes Lesson, AppointmentID and @AppointmentID become LessonID and @LessonID, and the sentence becomes Only an open lesson can be cancelled.

The change: keep the shape, change the names

The UPDATE still sets the status to Cancelled, and the row stays as history. Appointment becomes Lesson, and both ID names in the WHERE line change. Booked and Cancelled stay only if your own Status column allows those same words. END closes the stored procedure, and GO ends the batch.

blocks.p: Run your script after each stored procedure you add. If SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) shows an error, the last screen of this stage says what it means.

screens.title: Copy the C# for the same action and change its names.

blocks.p: Copy the Cancel method from AppointmentData, the bike shop's data class, into your own data class, such as LessonData. Then change the same names you changed in the stored procedure, so that the C# and the script agree: the program calls each stored procedure from a method like this one.

code.title: AppointmentData.Cancel: what changes and what stays
parts: public static string Cancel
public static string Cancel
The method: keep the action, change the ID

The method still returns a string: a blank one when it worked, or the refusal sentence. It goes in a data class called LessonData instead of AppointmentData, and appointmentID becomes lessonID in both places.
return Db.Run(
$end
The stored procedure name and its @ name: change both
The name inside Db.Run must be your own stored procedure's name, usp_Lesson_Cancel, letter for letter. The @ name inside Db.P must match the parameter at the top of that stored procedure, @LessonID.

blocks.p: A class in Models is copied the same way: copy the bike shop class, then change the class name and the property names to match your own columns. Screens are made new, the way chapter 6 made the customer screens, and then the code behind each one is copied from the bike shop screen and its names are changed.
Build after each file you copy, so that a name you missed shows up straight away, not ten files later.
A missed name is the most common fault when you copy. SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) and your program both say which name they cannot find, and each message below points at the line to fix.

wrong.q: SQL Server Management Studio says Invalid object name 'Appointment'.
wrong.a: A table name was not changed. Search the stored procedure for the bike shop table name and change every one, including the one after UPDATE.

wrong.q: SQL Server Management Studio says Invalid column name 'AppointmentID'.
wrong.a: A column name was not changed, most often in a WHERE line. Change it to your own column, such as LessonID.

wrong.q: SQL Server Management Studio says Must declare the scalar variable "@AppointmentID".
wrong.a: The @ name was changed at the top of the stored procedure but not lower down. Change every @ name to the same new name.

wrong.q: Your program shows the sentence Could not find stored procedure 'usp_Appointment_Cancel'.
wrong.a: The data class still calls the bike shop name. Change the name inside Db.Run to your own stored procedure's name.

wrong.q: A refusal sentence still talks about bikes or mechanics.
wrong.a: A sentence inside SET @Message was copied as it was. Read every sentence in your script and change its words to your case study.

blocks.p: When your own tables, stored procedures and screens all work, chapter 12 shows two upgrades that a case study can ask for. The fourteen checks in chapter 10 are the last thing you do before you hand in.
